title: trataka
hook: a candle on a low table, a dark room, and someone trying not to blink

segments.voice: Yesterday closed yoga nidra with the watcher, the one awake in those who sleep. In the middle of something busy, did you notice something in you stays awake? Today the eyes open. Day one thousand twenty-six.

A candle on a low table. The room is dark except for that one flame, about an arm's length away, level with the eyes. Someone sits in front of it, very still, looking. Not around it. At it. The flame leans, straightens, leans. The eyes start to sting. Then water. A tear runs down one cheek and the person still doesn't look away. This isn't a staring contest. It's a practice, written down in a manual of hatha yoga, and it has a name: today's word.
screen: `ONE FLAME IN A DARK ROOM.` → `LOOKING AT IT, NOT AROUND IT.` → `UNTIL THE TEARS COME.`

segments.voice: The Hatha Yoga Pradipika, a manual of hatha yoga, lists six cleansing acts in its second chapter, and trataka is one of them. Here's how the text describes it, in paraphrase: with a still mind, gaze with fixed eyes at a small mark, until tears come. The teachers, it says, call this trataka. So in the text, it isn't a candle exactly. It's a small point. A candle flame is one of the marks practitioners now use, and a dot on a wall is another. Then the text says what trataka does, in its own terms: it removes diseases of the eyes and drives away sloth, the heavy dullness that settles on a mind. And it adds a curious instruction: trataka should be guarded carefully, kept secret, like a casket of gold. Notice where it sits. It's grouped with the cleansing acts, practices of washing and clearing the body. Trataka cleans with attention. The eye, which spends the day darting from screen to face to sign to screen, is asked to do one thing and stay. And here's what makes this practice a turn from the last week. Yoga nidra lay down, closed the eyes, and drew the senses in. Trataka sits up and keeps the eyes open. It uses sight, a sense that pulls hard outward, and asks it to hold still on one small point until the mind holds still behind it. A word of care: teachers advise against staring at the sun or at anything harsh, and say to blink when the eyes ask. The text's tears are a sign of the gaze held, not a goal to strain for.
screen: `ONE OF SIX CLEANSING ACTS.` · `A STILL GAZE AT A SMALL MARK, UNTIL TEARS.` · `KEEP IT LIKE A CASKET OF GOLD.` · `EYES OPEN, THE MIND HELD STILL.` · then, large: `CLEANING WITH ATTENTION.`

segments.voice: Choose one small point in front of you, at eye level if you can: a mark on the wall, the tip of a pen, a candle flame if you have one safely lit. Never the sun. Sit comfortably and look at it. Not around it. At it. Let the eyes soften and stay. Blink when you need to; this is not a contest. When the eyes tire, close them, and watch whatever shape stays behind the lids until it fades. Then open them and look again. The bell holds the time.
Trataka. A still gaze at one small point, until the eyes water. In the Hatha Yoga Pradipika, one of the six cleansing acts.

Your line: cleaning with attention. Today, once, when you're waiting for something, pick a single small point and let your eyes rest on it for ten slow breaths instead of reaching for your phone. Day one thousand twenty-six.

howItsDone: Practitioners of hatha yoga do trataka by gazing steadily at a small point, often a candle flame at eye level in a dark room, then closing the eyes to hold the after-image; teachers advise against gazing at the sun.

notes: Editor pass: review updated for 1025's new carry; cut the unsourced superlative 'the sense that pulls us outward most'.
First day of the trataka block (1026–1032). This day sets the Hatha Yoga Pradipika's definition; later days can take the candle, the after-image (antar trataka), and links to dharana.

Paraphrase of HYP 2.31–32 (nirikshen nishchala-drisha sukshma-lakshyam samahitah, ashru-sampata-paryantam...; eye diseases, tandra; kept secret like a golden casket) and the list of six acts at 2.22. Pancham Sinh's 1914 translation exists but is not on the validator's list, so nothing is quoted.

The text's health claims (eye diseases) are reported as the text's own claims, not endorsed. Safety lines (no sun gazing, blink when needed) are general teacher guidance; confirm. Consider a note for people with eye conditions or seizure disorders.
Moving from yoga nidra to trataka is framed as eyes-closed to eyes-open; confirm the framing.
Audit: filler line ('it could be a scene from a film') replaced. HYP 2.22, 2.31–32 checked (small mark, until tears, eye diseases and tandra, golden casket).
